newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO heads, Yeltsin go to Paris for expansion deal.
newsitem.headline: NATO heads, Yeltsin go to Paris for expansion deal.

text.p: NATO leaders headed for Paris on Monday to sign a landmark treaty with Russia intended to lay the basis of a post-Cold War European security order and ease the alliance's expansion into former communist Europe.

Before leaving Moscow, President Boris Yeltsin -- who has had to accept he is powerless to stop at least a limited enlargement of the West's defence organisation -- talked tough, defending the accord as protecting Russia's interests.

He told Itar-Tass news agency in an interview that Moscow would not accept attempts to follow up membership for former Warsaw Pact countries by bringing in former Soviet republics, a clear reference to the three Baltic states.

"The negative consequences of expansion will be reduced to a minimum. This way we will not slip towards confrontation, which would inevitably involve big expenses for arms, a new militarisation of political thinking," he said.

Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic, three post-communist nations that formerly belonged to the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact, are expected to be offered NATO membership at an alliance summit in Madrid in July.
Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave of new entrants.

But under an historic security accord between the two former foes, Yeltsin has won assurances the allies have no plans to place nuclear weapons or foreign troops on the soil of the new members and has been granted a special consultative mechanism.

The "Founding Act on Mutual Relations, Cooperation and Security between NATO and the Russian Federation" sets up a NATO-Russia Council intended to give Russia a permanent voice in a new continent-wide security system for the 21st century.

Based at NATO's headquarters in Brussels, the Council will have a permanent secretariat and Russia will be represented by a permanent ambassador. Twice a year, it will meet at both foreign minister and defence minister level.
President Bill Clinton, who arrives in Paris early on Tuesday for the signing ceremony, has hailed the deal as "an historic step closer to a peaceful, undivided, democratic Europe".
But alliance diplomats say no amount of window-dressing can hide the fact that Yeltsin, under heavy criticism at home for the deal, failed to win a veto over future alliance activities.

Moscow is most concerned by the desire of some former Soviet republics, primarily the Baltic states Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia, to join the alliance and is angered by NATO's refusal to rule out future membership for them.
"I hope that through an open dialogue we will be able to convince those and other countries that their security will not increase by bringing them closer to NATO," Yeltsin said.
"I do not even allow a thought that such a dialogue would fail. This would fully undermine relations between Russia and NATO."

Clinton, a strong advocate of enlargement, sees the process as righting the wrongs of the Yalta conference at the end of World War Two when most of eastern Europe was left to come under the "zone of influence" of Josef Stalin's Soviet Union.

NATO intends to supplement enlargement and the deal with Russia with a revamped Partnership for Peace programme for other candidate countries in the hope that in time it will in itself satisfy their security concerns.
Diplomats say the Paris signing ceremony, a U.S. gesture to French President Jacques Chirac who is under fire for bringing his own country closer to NATO's military wing, will be largely ceremonial.
Earlier on Monday, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in Paris.
She was due to have lunch with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and then a private dinner with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
